 2                      I.   POSITION AND QUALIFICATIONS

 3   Q.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME, BUSINESS ADDRESS, AND CURRENT

 4        EMPLOYMENT POSITION.

 5   A.   My name is Collin M. Martin. I am employed by Oncor Electric Delivery

 6        Company LLC (“Oncor”). My business address is 777 Main Street Suite

 7        707, Fort Worth, TX 76102.      I hold the position of Vice President,

 8        Transmission and Distribution System Architecture. Before I took on that

 9        role in January 2026, I served as Vice President, Transmission Grid

10        Operations (“TGO”) and held other positions in the TGO group from 2018

11        to 2025.

12   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND AND

13        PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE.

14   A.   I hold a Bachelor of Science and a Master of Engineering in electrical

15        engineering from Texas A&M University and am a licensed Professional

16        Engineer in Texas. I have been employed by Oncor for 23 years in roles

17        spanning many aspects of engineering, operations, and support functions,

18        including System Protection, Transmission Operations, TGO, Asset

19        Management, Program Management, and Transmission Engineering. In

20        my time as Vice President of TGO, I was responsible for overseeing the

21        day-to-day, real-time operation of Oncor’s transmission system. A copy of

22        my resume is attached to my rebuttal testimony as Exhibit CMM-R-1.

  1   Q.   WHAT IS TGO’S ROLE IN THE DAY-TO-DAY OPERATION OF ONCOR’S

 2        TRANSMISSION SYSTEM?

 3   A.   TGO is responsible for the safe, reliable operation of Oncor’s transmission

 4        grid in coordination with the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc.

 5        (“ERCOT”) and other Transmission Operators across the ERCOT system.

 6        Oncor’s 24/7 control room operations staff monitor and control transmission

 7        and substation facilities to ensure equipment is loaded within the applicable

 8        ratings. The control room operations team is also responsible for managing

 9        transmission voltages and reactive reserves using available dynamic and

10        static reactive devices.

11               Following an outage on transmission or substation equipment,

12        control room staff responds by performing or directing the restoration of

13        service, thereby reducing customer outage time and restoring system

14        integrity. Oncor’s control room staff are required to exhibit competencies

15        for performing reliability-related tasks, obtaining certification from the North

16        American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”), maintaining that

17        certification through continued education and training. In addition, Oncor

18        has developed a robust training program that ensures all TGO personnel

19        are well trained in the skills required to perform their duties well. For control

20        room staff, this includes responding to system emergencies such as short

21        supply and “Black Start” conditions.

  1               Oncor’s support engineering staff are responsible for preparing

 2        procedures to guide control room staff in their response to various system

 3        emergencies. Support engineers also perform operational power-flow and

 4        contingency analysis studies of the transmission grid to assess system

 5        conditions, identify reliability issues and recommend solutions for resolving

 6        constraints. Oncor has implemented processes and procedures to ensure

 7        adherence to all regulatory and compliance obligations related to reliability

 8        and ERCOT market issues.

 9   Q.   HAVE YOU EVER SUBMITTED TESTIMONY BEFORE THE PUBLIC

10        UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS (“COMMISSION”)?

11   A.   Yes. I filed written testimony on behalf of Oncor in Docket Nos. 53601 and

13                   II.   PURPOSE OF REBUTTAL TESTIMONY

14   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

15   A.   The purpose of my rebuttal testimony is to respond to questions raised in

16        intervenor testimony regarding the need for the proposed Bell County East

17        Switch – Big Hill Substation 765 kilovolt (“kV”) transmission line project and

18        the proposed Big Hill Substation – Bell County East Switch 765 kV

19        transmission line project. Both projects are part of Import Path 2, as

20        identified by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (“ERCOT”) in the

21        Permian Basin Reliability Plan.



     ________________________________________________________________
     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                         Martin – Rebuttal
     PUC Docket No. 59475              Oncor Electric Delivery & LCRA TSC
                                           Bell County East – Big Hill CCN

                                            -4-                                        4
  1               More specifically, my rebuttal testimony addresses the assertion

 2        made by a number of intervenors, including intervenors such as Michael

 3        McWilliams, Tom Green, and Mark Friesenhahn, Jody Fauley, and others

 4        that Import Path 2 is either not necessary, will not be needed until 2038,

 5        and/or that local generation in Far West Texas is a viable substitute for

 6        Import Path 2. To illustrate why these claims are mistaken and provide

 7        important context regarding the need for the 765 kV import paths, my

 8        testimony describes ERCOT’s recent establishment of the North to Far

 9        West (“N-FW”) and South to Far West (“S-FW”) Generic Transmission

10        Constraints (“GTCs”), which I refer to collectively as the “Far West Import

11        GTCs.”

12               The Far West Import GTCs are two distinct system operating limits

13        (“SOLs”) on existing 345 kV transmission lines serving the Permian Basin

14        that, if exceeded, could result in firm load shed to avoid cascading power

15        outages across the entire West Texas transmission system. My rebuttal

16        testimony describes the conditions that gave rise to the Far West Import

17        GTCs, the practical and operational implications of the underlying

18        constraints, how the 765 kV import paths will help to resolve those system

19        limitations, and why ERCOT identified the Permian Basin 765 kV import

20        paths, including Import Path 2, as critical components of its exit strategy to

21        retire the Far West Import GTCs, with an expected in-service date of 2030.

     PUC Docket No. 59475              Oncor Electric Delivery & LCRA TSC

  1   Q.    WAS YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY PREPARED BY YOU OR UNDER

 2         YOUR DIRECT SUPERVISION AND CONTROL?

 3   A.    Yes.

 4        III.    FAR WEST TEXAS NEEDS ADDITIONAL IMPORT CAPACITY

 5   Q.    SOME INTERVENORS, INCLUDING TOM GREEN (PAGES 12-14, 113)

 6         AND RISA PAJESTKA (PAGE 5, LINE 20-PAGE 6, LINE 2) SUGGEST

 7         THAT IMPORT PATH 2 IS NOT NEEDED UNTIL 2038, IF AT ALL, AND

 8         SUGGEST DELAYING THE PROJECT. DO YOU AGREE?

 9   A.    No. And the ongoing reliability challenges in Far West Texas illustrate why

10         that is not the case. ERCOT’s Far West weather zone, which includes the

11         Permian Basin, faces a growing operational challenge driven by rapid load

12         growth, a lack of local thermal generation capacity, and operating limits on

13         the existing 345 kV import paths that serve the region. Peak demand

14         growth in the Far West has averaged 11% annually for the last decade, and

15         that growth is accelerating. Today, peak demand in the Far West weather

16         zone is approximately 9,800 MW, consisting primarily of commercial and

17         residential, oil and gas, and cryptocurrency/data center load. Much of this

18         load is "non-conforming," meaning its consumption is not dependent on the

19         weather or time of day. Thousands of MW of additional oil and gas and

20         data center load is already approved to energize or ramp up demand by the

21         end of 2026.

     PUC Docket No. 59475              Oncor Electric Delivery & LCRA TSC
                                           Bell County East – Big Hill CCN

                                           -6-                                        6
  1              Load-serving capabilities in Far West Texas depend on local

 2        generation capacity and the 345 kV transmission interfaces that allow power

 3        to be imported from the Panhandle, North, and Central Texas. The region

 4        currently has approximately 2,900 MW of installed thermal generation

 5        capacity, 7,000 MW of solar, 6,900 MW of wind, and 2,900 MW of energy

 6        storage resources (“ESRs”). Imports over the existing 345 kV interfaces

 7        are necessary to fully serve the customer demand in the Far West. As

 8        Oncor witness Mr. Jared Gurley explained in his direct testimony, ERCOT

 9        approved a number of 345 kV improvements to increase load-serving

10        capabilities over the last decade, but they have not kept pace with the fast-

11        growing demand—largely because of the long lead times for new

12        transmission infrastructure, the ability of customers to quickly build new

13        facilities, and uncertainty as to where new generation and customer load

14        will connect to the grid. Even with those improvements, the Far West region

15        experiences more transmission congestion than any other part of the

16        ERCOT system, often making it infeasible to plan outages of key

17        equipment, even for scheduled maintenance or construction.

18              Recent studies by both ERCOT and Oncor identified significant

19        SOLs that resulted in ERCOT establishing the Far West Import GTCs in

20        September 2025. A copy of the market notice announcing the Far West

21        Import GTCs is attached to my rebuttal testimony as Exhibit CMM-R-2.

  1   Q.   WHAT IS A GTC?

 2   A.   A GTC is a transmission constraint, consisting of one or more grouped

 3        transmission elements, that is used to manage power flows between

 4        geographic areas of the ERCOT system. Power flows over GTCs are

 5        monitored in real time and limited, as necessary, to prevent overloading and

 6        system instability.

 7   Q.   ARE THE FAR WEST IMPORT GTCS THE SAME AS THE GTC THAT

 8        MR. GURLEY DESCRIBED IN HIS DIRECT TESTIMONY?

 9   A.   No. The Far West Import GTCs are distinct from the West Texas Export

10        Interface GTC discussed in Mr. Gurley’s direct testimony. The West Texas

11        Export Interface constrains power flows out of Far West Texas, limiting the

12        amount of excess generation capacity that can be exported during periods

13        of high renewable output. In contrast, the Far West Import GTCs limit the

14        power that can be imported into Far West Texas to meet customer demand

15        when renewable output is low. The transmission elements that make up

16        the Far West Import GTCs are located further to the west, generally west of

17        a line extending from Abilene to Kerrville. The N-FW GTC includes the 345

18        kV transmission lines from Farmland – Long Draw, Long Draw – Scurry

19        County South, and Scurry County South – Faraday.          The S-FW GTC

20        includes the 345 kV transmission lines from Big Hill – Schneeman Draw,

21        Divide Switchyard – Sand Bluff, Cattleman Switch – Longshore Switch,

     PUC Docket No. 59475              Oncor Electric Delivery & LCRA TSC
                                           Bell County East – Big Hill CCN

                                          -8-                                        8
  1        Longshore Switch – Morgan Creek, Morgan Creek – Consavvy Switch, and

 2        Ranger Camp – Falcon Seaboard.

 3   Q.   WHY WAS IT NECESSARY FOR ERCOT TO ESTABLISH THE FAR

 4        WEST IMPORT GTCS?

 5   A.   ERCOT established the Far West Import GTCs to prevent uncontrolled

 6        thermal overloading and widespread power outages that are primarily at risk

 7        of occurring on nights with low wind, when there is no output from solar

 8        generation resources and little to no wind output. Under those conditions,

 9        the import capacity needed to serve the Far West customer load can exceed

10        the operating limits of the existing 345 KV import paths, even with all local

11        thermal resources operating at full capacity.          So far, the price-

12        responsiveness of crypto-miners and charging/discharging behavior of

13        batteries have provided some operating margin during constrained

14        conditions.   That is, when local generation cannot meet the Far West

15        demand, energy prices rise, batteries discharge, and price-responsive data

16        centers (i.e., crypto-miners) reduce their consumption. But this does not

17        eliminate the underlying deficit, which will continue to grow as new oil and

18        gas loads and non-price-sensitive data centers come online, leaving the

19        area at a continuous risk of pre-contingency firm load shed as an

20        emergency measure to prevent widespread power outages. Exhibit CMM-

21        R-3 to my rebuttal testimony is an ERCOT presentation from the February

22        Board of Directors meeting that describes these issues in detail.

  1   Q.   WHAT DO YOU MEAN BY "PRE-CONTINGENCY FIRM LOAD SHED"?

 2   A.   In practical terms, “pre-contingency firm load shed” means that on a night

 3        when wind generation is low and demand is high, utilities may be required

 4        to temporarily shut off power to customers, including homes, schools, and

 5        businesses, to protect the broader electric grid. Even though no equipment

 6        has failed and the system is otherwise functioning normally, if power flows

 7        over the Far West Import GTCs exceed their designated operating limits,

 8        ERCOT will direct electric utilities to interrupt service to customers to

 9        prevent the risk of widespread uncontrolled outages.

10   Q.   HOW ARE THE GTC LIMITS CALCULATED AND ENFORCED?

11   A.   GTC limits are calculated in real time based on prevailing system

12        conditions. When the GTC limits are at risk of being exceeded, ERCOT

13        must take corrective actions, which may include generation re-dispatch,

14        transmission reconfiguration, and ultimately firm load shed if other

15        measures are insufficient. In Far West Texas, the alternatives to firm load

16        shed are limited. Generation re-dispatch cannot solve the problem because

17        the issue stems from a localized generation deficit—there is ample

18        generation elsewhere on the system, but it cannot be delivered because the

19        import paths are at capacity. And transmission reconfiguration options are

20        generally ineffective due to the area-wide nature of the constraint. Attempts

21        to reconfigure the transmission system only push the constraint to other

22        facilities in West Texas but do not mitigate the constraint itself. This is a

  1        key characteristic of a GTC that must be managed at the interface level.

 2        When all of these alternatives are exhausted, if the GTC limits remain at

 3        risk of being exceeded, the only remaining action is shedding firm load to

 4        reduce the power flowing across the constrained interface and prevent

 5        cascading outages across the Far West region.

 6   Q.   HOW ARE THE FAR WEST TEXAS GTCS DIFFERENT THAN

 7        ORDINARY SOLS?

 8   A.   Under NERC Reliability Standard FAC-011-4, a SOL becomes an IROL if

 9        exceeding it would result in system instability or loss of load in excess of

10        2,000 MW due to cascading outages or voltage collapse. The Far West

11        Import GTCs were designated as IROLs because exceeding their

12        established operating limits could result in cascading thermal overloads

13        affecting the entire Far West region. The total load in that area already

14        exceeds 9,800 MW, so the 2,000 MW threshold is well within the bounds of

15        what could occur if the region experienced cascading outages.

16   Q.   WHAT DOES "CASCADING" MEAN IN THIS CONTEXT?

17   A.   Cascading is the uncontrolled, sequential loss of transmission elements,

18        resulting in a widespread power outage. To illustrate, imagine that one

19        transmission line that makes up the 345 kV interfaces experiences a fault

20        and is removed from service. The power that line was carrying does not

21        disappear;   it   instantaneously   redistributes   across   the   remaining

22        transmission lines that make up the interface. Because those lines are

  1        already operating near their thermal limits, this sudden influx causes them

 2        to overload or their protective relays to operate, removing those lines from

 3        service without any operator intervention.        Each successive outage

 4        accelerates the process because fewer lines are now carrying a growing

 5        share of the total import burden. Given the system configuration and small

 6        number of import paths serving Far West Texas, there is no natural stopping

 7        point for the outage short of a complete area blackout.

 8   Q.   WHAT IS THE CURRENT LOAD-SERVING CAPABILITY IN FAR WEST

 9        TEXAS UNDER CRITICAL CONDITIONS?

10   A.   With no solar output, low wind and ESR output, and thermal resources at

11        full capacity—the current maximum load-serving capability in Far West

12        Texas is approximately 9,500 MW. At that level, multiple constraints begin

13        approaching 125% of their maximum post-contingency loading, even when

14        the transmission system is fully intact and local thermal generation is fully

15        dispatched. This limit is lower if thermal generation is unavailable or if

16        transmission facilities are out of service.

17   Q.   HOW MUCH FIRM LOAD SHED WOULD BE REQUIRED IF THIS LEVEL

18        WERE EXCEEDED?

19   A.   The amount of potential load shed depends on a number of variables

20        including: wind conditions; the availability of dispatchable thermal resources

21        in the area; any transmission outages; load growth and the location of new

22        loads; prevailing weather conditions; battery behavior; and the behavior of

 2        scenarios will increase as load continues to grow in Far West Texas. This

 3        means the problem will worsen with every megawatt of new load that

 4        connects to the Far West transmission network.

 5   Q.   ARE NO-SOLAR, LOW-WIND CONDITIONS COMMON IN FAR WEST

 6        TEXAS?

 7   A.   Yes. Solar output drops to zero every night. Based on 2024 data, wind

 8        output is at or below 37% of capacity for half of nighttime hours (8 PM to

12   Q.   HOW DO THE FAR WEST TEXAS GTCS DIFFER FROM OTHER ERCOT

13        CONSTRAINTS LIKE THE SOUTH TEXAS EXPORT GTC?

14   A.   The Far West Import GTCs will overload when the Far West region does

15        not have sufficient local generation to serve the load in that area—even if

16        there is sufficient capacity elsewhere on the system. By contrast, the South

17        Texas Export GTC will only overload if the system as a whole does not have

18        sufficient capacity to serve the system load without using capacity south of

19        the constraint. In other words, the Far West Import GTCs represent a

20        localized energy deficit problem—the region needs more power delivered

21        to it than the existing transmission lines can physically carry, regardless of

22        how much generation is available elsewhere in Texas. This makes the

 3                    IV.   IMPORT PATH 2 IS NEEDED TODAY

 4   Q.   HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO INTERVENORS SUCH AS TOM GREEN

 5        AND MARK FRIESENHAHN (PAGE 10, LINES 21-23) WHO CLAIM THAT

 6        IMPORT PATH 2 IS NOT NEEDED AT THIS TIME?

 7   A.   As I explained above, the 765 kV import paths are needed to resolve system

 8        conditions that exist today. The Far West Import GTCs are evidence of this

 9        fact. Dating back to the 2024 Regional Transmission Plan, ERCOT has

10        stated that the 765 kV import paths are part of its “core plan” expected to

11        be in service in 2030. ERCOT’s April 2026 presentation on the Far West

12        Import GTC exit strategies underscores this point, showing an expected in-

13        service date of 2030 for the Permian Basin 765 kV import paths as part of

14        its plan to retire the Far West Import GTCs. A copy of that presentation is

15        attached as Exhibit CMM-R-5. Any delay of the 765 kV import paths would

16        prolong the Far West Import GTCs, subjecting the region to a continuing

17        and increasing risk of firm load shed to avoid cascading outages. While

18        other improvements like the Delaware Basin Stage 2 and Stage 5 345 kV

19        projects will provide incremental load-serving capability, those additions are

20        insufficient to keep pace with projected load growth.

 1   Q.   HOW WILL THE PROPOSED TRANSMISSION LINE PREVENT THE

 2        NEED FOR FIRM LOAD SHED?

 3   A.   The fundamental problem in Far West Texas is insufficient import capacity

 4        during hours when the region cannot generate enough electricity on its own.

 5        The 765 kV import paths directly address this problem in two ways. First,

 6        each 765 kV circuit will significantly increase the total import capacity

 7        available to Far West Texas. The 765 kV import paths represent by far the

 8        largest increase in import capacity on the planning horizon. Second, the

 9        presence of the 765 kV import paths will alter power flows to Far West

10        Texas, reducing the loading on the 345 kV import paths, providing additional

11        operating margins and allowing them to absorb more redistributed power

12        without becoming overloaded. With the 765 kV lines in service, the post-

13        contingency system can reach a stable state because the 765 kV pathways

14        will provide sufficient transfer capability to serve the Far West, even after

15        the loss of multiple 345 kV elements.

  1   Q.   ARE ANY INTERIM MITIGATION MEASURES BEING PURSUED UNTIL

 2        THE 765 KV IMPORT PATHS ARE IN SERVICE?

 3   A.   Yes. ERCOT and TSPs in the region are pursuing multiple mitigation

 4        activities until the 765 kV import paths are energized. These include

 5        implementing nighttime conductor ratings on critical lines to increase

 6        transfer capacity by taking advantage of cooler nighttime temperatures,

 7        pursuing a pilot application of dynamic conductor ratings, expanding remote

 8        load tap changer controls to facilitate additional voltage reduction

 9        capabilities, and assessing options to further accelerate delivery of projects

10        that will directly increase headroom to the GTC limits. These measures eke

11        out incremental gains from existing infrastructure, but they are interim
